summary: Gives guidelines for domain administrators who run a domain name server and look after their part of the hierarchical database. It assumes familiarity with the domain system as described in RFC 1031, RFC 1032, RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1033 gives domain administrators practical guidance for maintaining DNS zone data and operating a domain server. It explains common record types, timing values, reverse lookups, and routine update procedures.

subtitle: Operational guidance for domain administrators maintaining DNS zone data.

tldr.problem: Domain administrators need practical guidance for loading zone files, entering resource records, choosing timing values, and maintaining reverse lookups.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects operational notes on server startup, root-server information, record formats, common record types, TTLs, and procedures for adding or removing domains and hosts.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1033 is a guide that assumes familiarity with the domain system. It directs readers to the domain specifications for advanced details and notes that startup-file formats vary by implementation.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 1033's status as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text presents itself as operational notes and directs readers to RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 for advanced details.

sections.title: Zones and Server Startup
sections.content:
A zone is a contiguous part of the domain name space, usually separated by administrative boundaries. A zone file contains resource records for that part of the domain. A server's startup files identify the zones to load and provide a list of possible root servers.

The format of zone files is standardized, but startup files differ between server implementations. The RFC says that a server should contain data for domains it is authoritative for, with glue records as an exception. A resolver can contact a root server to obtain a current root-server list.
sections.plainLanguage: A zone file stores DNS records for a part of the domain name space. Server startup instructions identify which zone files and initial root-server information to load.

sections.title: Resource Records and Domain Names
sections.content:
A resource record contains a name, optional TTL, optional class, type, and data. Blank fields can inherit values from a preceding record or the zone's SOA record. Parentheses group records across lines, semicolons begin comments, and @ represents the current default domain.

A domain name is a sequence of labels separated by periods. An absolute name ends with a period; a relative name does not and receives the default domain. The RFC recommends a limited set of characters for host names because other protocols may impose restrictions.
sections.plainLanguage: A resource record states a name, record type, and data, with optional timing and class fields. A final period marks an absolute domain name; without it, the default domain is appended.

sections.title: TTL and the SOA Record
sections.content:
A Time to Live (TTL) is the number of seconds that a resolver may use a record before asking a server again. A short TTL causes more repeat requests; a long TTL delays the spread of changes. The RFC suggests setting most TTLs between one day (86400 seconds) and one week (604800 seconds), and lowering a value before a planned change.

The Start of Authority (SOA) record marks a zone and includes its serial number, refresh interval, retry interval, expiry time, and minimum TTL. The serial should increase when zone data changes. The RFC suggests 3600 seconds for refresh, 600 for retry, and 3600000 for expiry.
sections.plainLanguage: The TTL controls how long a resolver can reuse a record before checking again. SOA timing fields tell secondary servers when to refresh, retry, or stop using old zone data.

sections.title: Common Record Types
sections.content:
The guide describes common record types including SOA, NS, A, CNAME, HINFO, WKS, MX, and PTR. An NS record names a server for a domain; an A record gives a host's Internet address; and a CNAME maps a nickname to an official name. An MX record identifies where mail for a name should be delivered.

A PTR record supports reverse lookup in IN-ADDR.ARPA, which maps address components to names. The guide says to write the four address octets in reverse order for a host record. Gateway records can also identify a gateway by its network number.
sections.plainLanguage: Different DNS record types store addresses, aliases, mail destinations, and name-server information. PTR records support lookups that start with an address and return a name.

sections.title: Adding Hosts and Maintaining Zones
sections.content:
To add a subdomain, the administrator prepares its server or zone file, adds an NS record to the parent zone for each server, and adds any needed glue records. To add a host, the administrator adds records for each address and an appropriate reverse-lookup record for each address. Deleting a host removes its records from both forward and reverse zones.

The RFC includes a worked example for the SRI domain, with subdomains and forward and reverse zone files. It warns that the example data does not necessarily match actual data used by SRI. It also gives a suggested escalation order for reporting problems caused by another domain's server.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding or removing a host requires updating both its domain records and its reverse-lookup records. The sample zone files show one way the guide organizes these records.
